name: Tinchuley
tagline: Three hilltops, orange orchards and a quiet dawn over Kanchenjunga
meta_description: Tinchuley near Darjeeling: what the name means, Gumbadara viewpoint, orange orchards, village homestays from ₹1,500 pp, walks to Takdah and how to get there.
summary: Tinchuley is a small farming village at about 1,770 m, 32 km from Darjeeling and 3 km above Takdah. People come for the dawn view of Kanchenjunga from Gumbadara, walks through orange orchards and tea, and village homestays at ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals. One or two nights is enough.

local_story.title: Three clay stoves on a ridge above the Teesta
paras: The usual explanation of the name is simple and very hill-country. Tin is three, and chule comes from chulo, the clay cooking stove found in every village kitchen. Look at the ridge from below and, the local story goes, three rounded tops stand in a row like three stoves set side by side. Whether or not you can see it, the name tells you something about the people who gave it. This is a place named by farmers, after the thing at the centre of every home.

Tinchuley's families are mostly Nepali-speaking farmers who work these slopes for maize, millet, vegetables, cardamom in the shady hollows and, above all, oranges. The Darjeeling hills grow a small, thin-skinned mandarin, sweet with a sharp edge, and from November to January the orchards around the village colour up with it. Tea is part of the picture too: the village sits among the gardens of the Rangli Rangliot area, Rungli Rungliot and Gielle among them, and many households have someone working in the gardens.

In recent decades families here began opening rooms to guests, and Tinchuley became one of the early homestay names on Darjeeling itineraries. Today you sleep in a family room or a garden cottage, eat what the household eats and walk where they walk: up to the Gumbadara viewpoint at dawn, down through the orchards, across to the old British cantonment at Takdah. It is a small story, but it is the reason the village still looks and works like a village rather than a strip of hotels.

did_you_know: The local explanation of Tinchuley is 'three stoves': tin means three and chulo is the clay cooking stove, after three rounded hilltops said to stand in a row on the ridge.
From the Gumbadara viewpoint above Tinchuley the view runs north to Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m and the third-highest mountain on Earth, and east into the Teesta valley.
Tinchuley, at about 1,770 m, is only about 3 km from Takdah, a cantonment the British army set up in the early 1900s, and roughly 32 km by road from Darjeeling.
intro: Tinchuley is a village first and a destination second, which is why people like it. The road ends among houses, cow sheds, terraced fields and orange trees, and the homestays are part of family homes rather than a row of lodges. At about 1,770 m it is warmer than Darjeeling and cooler than the valley below. On clear mornings Kanchenjunga stands over the ridges to the north and the Teesta valley drops away to the east. By 9 am the cloud often rises, and the day turns to walking, eating and sitting in the sun.

Most visitors arrive on a car loop from Darjeeling with Lamahatta and Takdah, and many make it a day trip. Stay the night instead. Dawn at Gumbadara is the reason to come, and you cannot do it from Darjeeling without leaving at 4.30 am. Homestays charge ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Bring cash, a torch and warm clothes from November to February, when nights fall to roughly 3–6 °C and rooms without heaters feel colder than that.
facts: Jio and Airtel in most of the village
costs: Reserved car from Darjeeling, one way
Reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra
Village companion for a half-day walk
Tea and biscuits in a village shop

highlights.title: Dawn at Gumbadara
highlights.text: The village viewpoint looks north to Kanchenjunga and east into the Teesta valley. Aim to be there 20–30 minutes before sunrise between October and April for the best chance of clear peaks. Bring a flask and a warm jacket; there is nothing to buy at the top, only the view.

highlights.title: Orange orchards in winter
highlights.text: From November to January the slopes around the village fill with small Darjeeling mandarins. Walk the lanes between the orchards, watch families pick and sort the fruit, and buy a bag if someone offers. Mornings are sunny and dry, and the colour against the dark green is reason enough to come.

highlights.title: The walk to Takdah
highlights.text: Three kilometres down the road to the old British cantonment, with its bungalows, pines and orchid centre. About 45 minutes down and an hour back up. It is the easiest way to see both villages, and on the way you pass farmhouses, tea plots and terraced fields rather than shops.

highlights.title: A small village monastery
highlights.text: Tinchuley has a small Buddhist monastery that serves the families around it. It is no Ghoom or Rumtek, which is its charm. Visit quietly in the morning, walk clockwise around it, ask before taking pictures inside and leave a small donation.

highlights.title: Home-cooked hill food
highlights.text: Homestay meals are the family's own food: rice, dal, a vegetable from the garden, a pickle, sometimes squash shoots, local greens or chicken. Ask for gundruk soup or sel roti if they are being made. Dinner and breakfast are in the rate, and an extra lunch costs ₹150–250.

highlights.title: Tea gardens on the slopes
highlights.text: Tinchuley lies among the tea gardens of the Rangli Rangliot area, with Rungli Rungliot and Gielle within walking or short-drive distance. Garden roads make good half-day walks from March to November, when pluckers are at work in the mornings.

how_to_reach.text: From Darjeeling, go via Ghoom and Jorebunglow onto the Peshok road, past Lamahatta, then turn off for Takdah and Tinchuley: about 32 km, 1.5–2 hours. One way costs ₹2,000–2,800; a day loop with Lamahatta and Takdah is ₹2,500–4,000. From NJP or Bagdogra expect ₹3,800–4,800 and about 4 hours.

Shared jeeps to this side are few. Ask at Darjeeling's motor stand about jeeps for Takdah, which may carry on to Tinchuley, or take a Kalimpong-bound jeep to the Takdah turning and have your homestay send a car for the last stretch. Seats cost roughly ₹100–150; check current status before you travel.

From Siliguri you can come up the Teesta valley to Teesta Bazar and climb via Peshok, a route about as long as going through Darjeeling. The Teesta valley road (NH10) has had repeated closures since the October 2023 flood: check current status before you travel.
If you are staying in Takdah, walk the 3 km road up to Tinchuley in about an hour, with tea in the village and the Gumbadara viewpoint at the top.

where_to_stay: Tinchuley is a homestay village. You stay in family houses, garden cottages or newer rooms built beside the family home, almost all with dinner and breakfast included at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person. Houses near the top of the village are closer to the Gumbadara viewpoint for dawn; those lower down are quieter and nearer the orchards and the road to Takdah. Your host can usually arrange cars for transfers. We do not name individual homestays because standards change; ask for recent photos of the room and bathroom, whether there is a heater, and how far the house is from the road with luggage.
tips: Stay at least one night, because dawn at Gumbadara is the reason to come and day trippers miss it.
Visit from November to January for oranges and clear skies, and pack warm layers for nights of roughly 3–6 °C.
Carry cash for your stay, since card payment and ATMs are not something to count on in the village.
Ask your homestay to book your return car the evening before, especially if you have a train or flight to catch.
Buy oranges and vegetables from the families who grow them; it is the most direct way your money stays in the village.

experiences.title: Dawn over Kanchenjunga from Gumbadara
experiences.summary: A short pre-dawn walk from your homestay to Tinchuley's Gumbadara viewpoint, where the first sun hits Kanchenjunga to the north and mist fills the Teesta valley to the east. No crowds, no ticket and no 4 am jeep.
body: Tiger Hill is famous for its sunrise, and in October and May it is also famous for its crowds. Tinchuley offers a smaller, quieter version. From the Gumbadara viewpoint above the village, the Kanchenjunga massif stands to the north, 8,586 m at its summit and the third-highest mountain on Earth. The peaks catch the first light pink and gold while the ridges in front are still dark, and below to the east the Teesta valley lies under a layer of mist that slowly burns off as the sun climbs.

Ask your homestay the evening before how long the walk takes from the house, and set out so you arrive 20–30 minutes before sunrise. In November that means leaving around 5 am. Carry a torch, a warm jacket, a hat and a flask of tea, because you will be standing still in the cold. The way up is short, but walk slowly in the dark and watch your footing. If you have children with you, the top is open ground, so keep them close near the edges.

Clear mornings are most likely from October to early December and again in March and April. In the monsoon you may see nothing at all, and in late spring haze often hides the peaks. Give yourself two mornings if you can. When the view fails, the walk still pays: you watch the village wake up, smoke rise from kitchen fires and the first jeeps start down the road. Back at the homestay, breakfast will be waiting, and it tastes better for the cold.

faqs.q: What time should we leave for Gumbadara?
faqs.a: Aim to arrive 20–30 minutes before sunrise. That means leaving your homestay around 5 am in October and November, about 5.30 am in December and January, and earlier, around 4.30 am, in April. Ask your host for the walking time from your house, which varies across the village.

faqs.q: Is the Gumbadara sunrise better than Tiger Hill?
faqs.a: It is different. Tiger Hill is higher, at about 2,567 m, and on very clear days shows Everest far to the west. Gumbadara is lower but quiet, close to your bed and free. If crowds bother you or you dislike 4 am jeep rides, Tinchuley's dawn is the better morning. Many travellers do both on one trip.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide to reach the viewpoint?
faqs.a: No. The viewpoint is close to the village and your homestay will explain the way. In the dark, though, it helps to walk it once the afternoon before so you know the turns. If your host or a family member offers to walk up with you, ₹200–300 is a kind thank-you.

experiences.title: Orange orchards of Tinchuley in winter
experiences.summary: A slow late-morning walk through the orchards around Tinchuley between November and January, when the small, sweet Darjeeling mandarins ripen. Meet the growers, taste fruit if offered and see how a hill farm actually works.
body: Long before tea and tourism, the slopes below Darjeeling were farmed for food, and oranges have long been part of that. The Darjeeling mandarin is small, thin-skinned and sweet with a sharp edge, and it grows well on the warmer middle slopes of these hills. Around Tinchuley, orange trees stand in terraced orchards, at the edges of maize fields and right beside houses. From November to January the fruit colours up, and the whole hillside changes from dark green to green flecked with orange.

There is no set route and no ticket. Leave your homestay in late morning, when the sun is up and the chill has gone, and follow the lanes and field paths down through the orchards. Ask your host to point you toward families who do not mind visitors. You will see fruit picked by hand, sorted into baskets and carried up to the road on people's backs. Much of the crop is sold to traders and sent down to markets in the plains, so the harvest weeks are busy ones.

Be a good guest. Stay on paths, ask before you enter an orchard and never pick fruit without being invited. If a family offers you oranges, accept and offer to pay; it will cost little and they may refuse, but the gesture matters. Buy a bag to take home if they sell to you. In a poor year, after hail or disease, there may be little fruit, so ask your homestay how the season is going before you plan a trip around it.

faqs.q: When is orange season in Tinchuley?
faqs.a: Roughly November to January, with the best fruit usually in December. Timing shifts each year with rain and temperature, and a bad hailstorm can damage a crop. Ask your homestay a week or two before your trip how the season looks, and treat oranges as a bonus rather than a certainty.

faqs.q: Can we buy oranges directly from the farmers?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Families with a good crop will usually sell a bag to visitors at a fair local price, lower than you pay in Darjeeling. Ask politely, carry small notes and do not haggle hard. If a family says no, they may already have sold the whole crop to a trader.

faqs.q: Is the orchard walk suitable for older people?
faqs.a: Partly. The lanes near the road are gentle, but field paths between terraces are narrow, uneven and steep in places. Older travellers can enjoy the orchards along the village road and the homestay garden without going far down. Good shoes and a walking stick help on the steeper bits.

experiences.title: Village monastery and a morning in Tinchuley
experiences.summary: An unhurried hour at Tinchuley's small Buddhist monastery and the lanes around it: prayer flags, morning offerings and the village starting its day. A quiet counterpoint to the big, busy monasteries of Ghoom and Kalimpong.
body: The monasteries people travel to in these hills are big ones: Yiga Choeling at Ghoom, founded in 1850, or Zang Dhok Palri in Kalimpong. Tinchuley's monastery is a different thing, a small village gompa that serves the Buddhist families of the area. That is exactly why it is worth an hour. There is no ticket booth, no tour group and no gift shop, only the prayer hall, the prayer flags snapping in the wind and whoever happens to be there that morning.

Go early, between about 7 and 9 am, when lamps may be lit and a monk or caretaker may be making the morning offerings. Take off your shoes at the door, walk clockwise around the building, and do not point your feet at the altar if you sit down. Ask before taking photographs inside; a nod usually means yes, a shake means put the phone away. Leave ₹20–100 in the donation box, which helps with lamps and upkeep.

Then walk back slowly through the village. Mornings in Tinchuley are working time: cows being milked and led out, children in uniform heading for the school jeep, people carrying fodder up the slopes and smoke rising from kitchens. Greet people with a namaste, keep out of the way and do not photograph children without asking a parent. You learn more about how a hill village lives in this hour than on any viewpoint.

faqs.q: Is Tinchuley's monastery open to visitors?
faqs.a: Generally yes, in the daytime, and visitors are welcome if they are quiet and respectful. A small village gompa has no fixed visiting hours, so the hall may be locked at times. Early morning is the best chance to find someone there; ask your homestay who looks after it.

faqs.q: What should we wear to the monastery?
faqs.a: Ordinary modest clothes are fine: covered shoulders and knees, nothing too tight or revealing. You will take your shoes off at the door, so socks are useful on cold mornings. Remove hats inside the prayer hall. No special dress is expected of visitors, only quiet behaviour.

faqs.q: Can we attend a puja or festival there?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Village monasteries hold prayers on full-moon days, at Losar in February or March and on other dates in the Tibetan calendar. Ask your homestay whether anything is planned during your stay. If you are invited, sit at the back, follow what others do and offer a small donation.

experiences.title: Cook a hill dinner in a homestay kitchen
experiences.summary: Join your homestay family in the kitchen for an evening: chopping greens, cooking dal and rice, and learning what gundruk and chhurpi are. Arranged with your host on the spot, never a fixed class, and the best food lesson in the hills.
body: Food in Tinchuley follows the farm and the season. Dinner at a homestay is usually rice, dal, a vegetable or two from the garden, a pickle and sometimes chicken, with squash shoots, fiddlehead ferns (ningro) or nettle (sisnu) when they are in season. Gundruk, leafy greens fermented and dried, turns up in soups and pickles through the winter. These are not restaurant dishes. They are what the family eats, and the best way to understand them is to stand beside the stove while they are made.

Ask your host when you book, or on your first evening, whether you can join them in the kitchen. Many families are happy to, especially outside the busiest weeks. You might wash and chop greens, grind chillies and tomatoes for a pickle, watch rice cook and dal simmer, and learn how gundruk is soaked and turned into a sour soup. If your visit falls around Dashain or Tihar, you may see sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread, fried for the festival. Do not expect printed recipes; this is family cooking.

Agree in advance whether there is an extra charge. Often there is none, since you will eat the meal anyway; some families ask ₹300–600 for the time and extra ingredients, which is fair. Bring nothing but curiosity and a willingness to wash up. If you have food allergies or do not eat meat, say so early. Write down what you learn, because the same dish can be made three different ways in three houses on the same ridge.

faqs.q: Do homestays in Tinchuley serve vegetarian food?
faqs.a: Yes. Most homestay meals are largely vegetarian anyway, built on rice, dal, vegetables and pickles, with meat as an extra. Tell your host when you book if you are vegetarian, vegan or avoid eggs, onion or garlic, so they can plan. Jain food is harder to arrange, so give clear notice.

faqs.q: What is gundruk?
faqs.a: Gundruk is leafy greens, usually mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, that are wilted, packed tight to ferment for some days and then sun-dried. It keeps for months and goes into a sour soup and into pickles, especially in winter. It is one of the signature foods of Nepali kitchens across these hills.

faqs.q: Is there an extra charge to cook with the family?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Many hosts will let you help for free, since the meal is already part of your rate. Others ask ₹300–600 for the extra time or special ingredients, for example when making sel roti. Agree it before you start and pay the host directly. Never treat it as a guaranteed activity.

faqs.q: How far is Tinchuley from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 32 km, 1.5–2 hours by car via Ghoom, Jorebunglow and the Peshok road past Lamahatta and Takdah. A reserved car costs ₹2,000–2,800 one way, or ₹2,500–4,000 for a day loop. Shared jeeps rarely come all the way, so plan on a car for at least the last stretch.

faqs.q: What does the name Tinchuley mean?
faqs.a: The common local explanation is 'three stoves': tin is three in Nepali and chulo is the clay cooking stove. People say three rounded hilltops on the ridge look like three stoves set side by side. It is a folk explanation rather than a documented history, but you will hear it from almost everyone in the village.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Tinchuley?
faqs.a: October to early December for clear Kanchenjunga mornings, and November to January for oranges. March and April are mild, with flowers and fair views. The monsoon, June to September, brings heavy rain, mist and leeches, though prices soften. December and January nights are cold, roughly 3–6 °C.

faqs.q: Is Tinchuley worth staying a night?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want a quiet village, a dawn view without crowds and home-cooked food. There are no shops, ticketed sights or nightlife. The main reason to stay is to be at Gumbadara for sunrise, which day trippers from Darjeeling miss. One night is enough; two lets you walk to Takdah and the tea gardens.

faqs.q: How much do homestays in Tinchuley cost?
faqs.a: Most charge about ₹1,500–2,500 per person per night with dinner and breakfast, sometimes less in the monsoon and more around Durga Puja, Diwali and New Year. Children usually pay less. Ask whether the rate includes tea, lunch and transfers, and carry cash for payment.

faqs.q: Can we see Kanchenjunga from Tinchuley?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings, mainly from October to early December and in March and April, from the Gumbadara viewpoint and open spots in the village. Cloud usually builds by mid-morning. In the monsoon the peaks are hidden most days, and in late spring haze often softens the view.

faqs.q: Is Tinchuley good for a budget honeymoon?
faqs.a: It suits couples who like quiet. A homestay room for two with meals costs roughly ₹3,000–5,000 a night, the dawn walk is short and lovely, and evenings are calm. Choose a house with an attached bathroom and a heater in winter, and pair it with a night or two in Darjeeling.

faqs.q: Can we combine Tinchuley with Takdah and Lamahatta?
faqs.a: Easily. Lamahatta is on the Peshok road on the way, and Takdah is 3 km below Tinchuley. A good plan is Lamahatta as a stop on the drive, two nights in Tinchuley and a morning walk to Takdah's bungalows and orchid centre. A car from Darjeeling for the loop costs ₹2,500–4,000.

faqs.q: Is there internet and electricity in Tinchuley?
faqs.a: Yes, both, with interruptions. Jio and Airtel work in most of the village, though signal varies from house to house. Power cuts happen, more often in storms and the monsoon. Carry a power bank and a torch, and download maps and tickets before you arrive.
